name: Hana Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the labeler for medicine bottles and check batch and expiry on the first tray. I have a vocational machine certificate, years on the line and about average skill for an experienced operator. A wrong expiry is not an experiment for the customer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Amir works at a repair shop and our grown children have their own homes. We have a house loan, four months saved, my typical operator pay and some similar factories nearby. I use AI every day to sort shift notes, then compare it with the paper run sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little AI help with schedules is fine. I still check the first tray of medicine bottles for the right batch and expiry before the labeler runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband Amir earns at a repair shop, and both wages cover our house loan. Our grown children are on their own, four months saved is useful, and I am an ordinary experienced operator rather than the quality manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the labeler shift, compare my daily AI note summary with the paper run sheet, and pay extra loan principal from fresh full wages after bills. I would leave the existing reserve where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be calm. Sunday dinner can be about family rather than a machine nobody has ordered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can go wrong on the first tray?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An expiry can be one digit wrong even when the label looks straight. The printed order, not an AI summary, tells me what belongs on the bottle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does extra loan money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From this month’s wages after ordinary bills. I would not call the four months already saved a new deposit.

I would verify **daily AI notes** against printed orders.
think: Our **two wages** cover current loan payments and ordinary household bills.
A **four-month reserve** offers room for a brief setback at the plant.
do: Keep **labeler shifts** and verify batch and expiry.
Compare **existing AI notes** with the printed run sheet.
Pay extra **loan principal** from fresh full wages after bills.
feel: **Calm** about present work and covered household bills.

fieldNote: Her **vocational certificate** and years of labeler experience support average mid-level machine skill.
Daily **AI notes** are existing use; extra debt payment comes only from newly earned full wages.

steps.text: Keep medicine-labeler shifts and verify first-tray batch and expiry
Pay extra house-loan principal from fresh full wages after bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office software can move quickly, but a camera beside medicine labels needs a careful trial. I would like to learn it early if the plant offers safe paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A vision camera could take my simple first-tray work and cut my shift. Four months saved would not cover a long wage gap, even with Amir still employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request an offered paid practice slot on rejected bottles with the conveyor isolated and the setter present. If approved, I would learn the new AI vision threshold against the printed order; after actual hour cuts, I would apply for posted reachable packaging work only where net pay after travel covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about paid hours, though curious about the camera. A practice bottle is the place to find a wrong expiry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you use a live line to practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The setter must isolate the conveyor and give me a real paid slot before I touch the controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would another plant guarantee work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. There are some nearby, but only an actual posting, wage and travel calculation would tell us whether a move helps.

fieldNote: She is **adaptive** but needs an offered paid isolated practice slot before using controls.
Outside **job applications** require actual cuts, reachable postings and adequate net pay after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2028 finds me sixty; capable bottle-handling robots around 2031 find me sixty-three. The office changes first, and then the line may need fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the rebuilt labeler to remove most of my paid shifts. Amir’s repair wage and four months saved will not carry the house loan indefinitely, and I wake early thinking about the next payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for written staffing dates and postpone the kitchen extension. I would apply for posted reachable operator jobs with bill-covering net pay after travel, and would not leave this shift before a real offer and start date; if the shift ends without one, I would ask the lender about temporary terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by the likely wage loss. A mortgage letter does not care how clever the labeler has become.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop work at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if verified retirement and household income covered the loan, food and health costs. We have not priced that, so I expect to keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your children pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes. A lift to an interview might help, but their wages are not ours.

I would keep **label safety** in the plant plan.

The **loan and four-month reserve** make that a major income loss.

feel: **Alarmed** and waking early over expected major wage loss.
S2.quote: A mortgage letter does not care how clever the labeler has become.
fieldNote: Expected **large shift loss** supports alarm despite her partner’s wage.

steps.text: Apply for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay operator job before leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2031 reaches me at sixty-three, and bottle-handling robots around 2034 at sixty-six. Five years could support a real quality course instead of a glossy advertisement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I enjoy new tools, but quality work needs a recognised certificate and supervised bottle sampling. Unpaid class hours would strain the house loan, and a job must exist nearby at a wage that works after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid labeler shift and ask for a funded course on paid time. If offered an actual place with isolated-machine sampling supervised by a qualified tester and a posted reachable quality role at bill-covering net pay, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for that role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about later shifts but pleased to compare real course terms. I would not buy a certificate on the strength of a bright brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would sample rejected bottles and record why an expiry or seal failed, with the conveyor stopped and a tester supervising. That would give me a real fault to explain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If no place opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid shifts and search posted operator openings if hours fell. I would not spend our four-month reserve on private fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight and capable bottle robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. Ten years lets Amir and me put real numbers beside a last factory day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had hoped to finish full-time shifts at sixty-seven, but four months saved is not retirement income. I do not know any pension amount or Amir’s future wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the labeler shift and pay extra loan principal from fresh wages after bills. I would request retirement and loan figures; if verified income covers housing, food and health costs at sixty-seven I would stop factory work then, otherwise continue safe paid work, and after 2036 seek posted reachable bill-covering work only if still employed and hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about distant robots while current wages cover our bills. I want a last shift I can tell the children about without asking them to pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the figures are short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep safe paid work and compare posted jobs after travel if hours fell. A birthday cannot pay the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children fund the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They have their own homes, and I will not put their wages in our calculation.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because bottle-handling robots around 2031 could take most of my shift while the loan remains. Written staffing dates, offered funded safe paid quality training and posted work with adequate net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs the first tray when a label changes. I can welcome a camera and still put my own name beside a checked bottle.

headlineQuote: I can welcome a camera and still put my own name beside a checked bottle.
portrait: **Hana**, 58, is an experienced mid-level medicine-labeler operator with vocational certification and average skill.
She has **typical pay**, repair-shop husband Amir, grown children, a loan, four months saved and some nearby factories.
She uses **AI daily** and would learn new vision controls through offered paid safe practice.
Fast **2031 robot cuts** alarm her; a planned age-sixty-seven exit needs verified income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because 2031 robots may take most paid labeler shifts while the loan remains.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered funded safe paid instruction and posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work would help.
